title: Sylow's Theorems
description: The three Sylow theorems: existence of Sylow p-subgroups, their conjugacy, and counting constraints. Fundamental structure theorems for finite groups.

meta.author: Peter Ludwig Mejdell Sylow (formalized via Mathlib)

mathlibDependencies.description: Number of Sylow subgroups is congruent to 1 mod p

originalContributions: Pedagogical statement of all three Sylow theorems
Proof that unique Sylow subgroups are normal
Cauchy's theorem as a corollary of Sylow I

overview.historicalContext:
Peter Ludwig Mejdell Sylow (1832-1918) was a Norwegian mathematician who spent most of his career as a high school teacher in Halden, proving these landmark theorems as a side pursuit. He published them in *Mathematische Annalen* (1872, vol. 5) — a single paper that transformed finite group theory.

Georg Frobenius (1849-1917) gave streamlined alternative proofs in 1887 and strengthened the counting theorem. William Burnside (1852-1927) deployed Sylow's theorems extensively, proving in 1904 that all groups of order p^a·q^b are solvable — a result later reproved by Feit-Thompson (1963) as part of the monumental Odd Order Theorem.

The theorems became a cornerstone of the Classification of Finite Simple Groups (CFSG), completed ~2004 by Aschbacher, Smith, and others: Sylow counting immediately eliminates most orders from being simple, while conjugacy ensures uniform subgroup structure within each prime family.
overview.problemStatement:
**The Three Sylow Theorems** for a group G of order n = p^k * m where p is prime and p does not divide m:

1. **Existence**: G has a subgroup of order p^k (Sylow p-subgroup)
2. **Conjugacy**: All Sylow p-subgroups are conjugate to each other
3. **Counting**: The number n_p of Sylow p-subgroups satisfies: n_p divides m and n_p ≡ 1 (mod p)

This is Wiedijk's 100 Theorems #72.
overview.proofStrategy:
**Sylow I (Existence)**:
Use induction on |G| and analyze the class equation.

**Sylow II (Conjugacy)**:
Let P act on cosets G/Q by multiplication and use orbit-stabilizer.

**Sylow III (Counting)**:
P acts on the set of Sylow p-subgroups by conjugation; the only fixed point is P itself.
keyInsights: Existence (Sylow I) is proved via the class equation |G| = |Z(G)| + Σ|Cl(x)|: either the center Z(G) has an element of order p (Cauchy applied to the abelian center), or some conjugacy class has size not divisible by p, providing a proper subgroup on which to apply induction

Conjugacy (Sylow II) follows from orbit-stabilizer: let P act on cosets G/Q; if P ≠ Q then |P∩Q| < |P|, so every P-orbit on G/Q has size > 1; but P is a p-group so all orbit sizes are p-powers, meaning |G/Q| ≡ 0 mod p — contradicting |G/Q| = m where p ∤ m, so P = gQg⁻¹

The counting constraints n_p ≡ 1 (mod p) and n_p | m severely limit possible group structures: for |G| = 15 both constraints force n_3 = n_5 = 1, so every group of order 15 is cyclic — a complete classification from arithmetic alone

Unique Sylow subgroups are automatically normal: n_p = 1 means the subgroup is its own unique conjugate, i.e., gPg⁻¹ = P for all g ∈ G — this equivalence (n_p = 1 ⟺ P ⊴ G) is the primary way normality is established in classification arguments

Sylow's theorems are a blueprint for the Classification of Finite Simple Groups: any simple group must have n_p > 1 for every prime p dividing its order (otherwise a normal Sylow subgroup exists), and Sylow counting constraints then force |G| to be extremely large — ruling out all 'small' orders from being simple

sections.title: First Sylow Theorem (Existence)
sections.summary: For any prime p, a finite group has at least one Sylow p-subgroup.
sections.mathContext: Sylow I: $p^a \mid |G| \Rightarrow \exists H \leq G$ with $|H| = p^a$. Proved by the class equation or by counting fixed points of $G$ acting on subsets.

sections.title: Second Sylow Theorem (Conjugacy)
sections.summary: All Sylow p-subgroups are conjugate to each other.
sections.mathContext: Sylow II: All Sylow $p$-subgroups are conjugate: $P, Q$ Sylow $\Rightarrow \exists g \in G,\; gPg^{-1} = Q$. In particular, $n_p = [G : N_G(P)]$.

sections.title: Third Sylow Theorem (Counting)
sections.summary: The number of Sylow p-subgroups is congruent to 1 mod p.
sections.mathContext: Sylow III: $n_p \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$ and $n_p \mid m$ where $|G| = p^a m$. Combined with Sylow II: $n_p = [G : N_G(P)]$.

sections.title: Uniqueness and Normality
sections.summary: A unique Sylow p-subgroup is normal.

sections.title: Cauchy's Theorem
sections.summary: If p divides |G|, then G has an element of order p.

conclusion.summary: The Sylow theorems are indispensable for understanding finite group structure. They combine existence, uniqueness up to conjugacy, and counting constraints into a powerful toolkit for analyzing groups.
conclusion.implications:
**Applications:**

**1. Groups of order pq**
Sylow shows n_q = 1 when q > p.

**2. Groups of order p^2**
Must be abelian.

**3. Simple group classification**
Rules out many possible orders.

**4. Burnside's theorem**
Groups of order p^a * q^b are solvable.
openQuestions: Generalizations to profinite and infinite groups

crossReferences.description: Lagrange's theorem (|H| divides |G|) is the foundation — Sylow theorems provide a partial converse: for prime power divisors, subgroups of that order exist
Sylow subgroups help determine composition factors of S_n, relevant to the solvability analysis in Abel-Ruffini
Sylow theory constrains which groups can be Galois groups — the structure of Sylow subgroups determines embedding problems in inverse Galois theory
